title: Nirtshe: a Jewish settlement on the river route
summary: Nirtshe shows how Jewish settlement, farming, trade, and river traffic extended beyond the town itself.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Founding of the Jewish settlement at Nirtshe

editorialContent:
## A settlement at the water’s edge

The Jewish settlement of Nirtshe grew up not as a second David-Horodok, but as a small community shaped by the river, the land and the traffic between them. The memorial book places [Nirtshe](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_98cc0690f4a5beb7cb0e174f) near the Horyn’s mouth, where it flows into the Pripyat, about twelve kilometres from [David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_bcbe8f6f5fb9a4059354cafb). That location connected the settlement to an active route of boats, rafts and passengers—and gave its residents work beyond farming.

The book’s accounts do not settle on one precise founding year. One record says the settlement was founded in the early nineteenth century; another places its founding after 1812, while explicitly noting that the exact date is uncertain. The Yiddish account likewise describes a Jewish settlement arising at the beginning of the nineteenth century. Taken together, these testimonies support a broad dating, not a single year. The book identifies the [Morbatshik family](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_eee0c297188f9371426d753e) with the settlement’s beginnings, and names Yosel Morbatshik as its founding figure.

The wider sources consulted do not independently document Nirtshe’s founding or the Morbatshik family’s history. The specific account of its origins, livelihood and eventual dissolution therefore rests on the memorial book’s testimony, not on a separate archival confirmation.

## Land, timber and river trade

The memorial book portrays the Morbatshiks as neither exclusively farmers nor simply merchants. Their livelihood combined horticulture, fishing, cattle raising and commerce—especially in lumber and wooden goods. They worked their gardens themselves and hired both peasants and merchants. They also supplied food to workers travelling on steamships, rafts and other river craft, and prepared meals for passengers. Their work tied the settlement to people passing through as well as to the surrounding countryside.

Timber was both a local resource and a trade good. The book recalls that the family hauled firewood by transport vessels toward Kyiv. The [Horyn River](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_9085c65655ce02127c85e577) joins the [Pripyat River](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_04b3f73bd3fe9f4585769a1e); the Horyn’s course and confluence are also described in the [Wikipedia entry on the river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horyn). The Pripyat, in turn, runs through the forested wetlands of Polesia, as summarized in the [Wikipedia entry on the Pripyat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pripyat). These geographical sources help clarify why water transport mattered in this landscape, but they do not independently verify the book’s account of Nirtshe’s particular trade.

The wider regional picture makes the book’s description plausible without proving every detail. Forest products and river transport were important to commerce in the Pripyat basin. But Nirtshe’s distinctive economic arrangement—as remembered by its former neighbours—was the Morbatshiks’ combination of cultivation, trade, timber hauling and hospitality to river workers and passengers. In the book’s telling, river traffic was not an abstract route on a map: it brought customers, workers and travellers close to home.

## A community connected to David-Horodok

The memorial book calls Nirtshe’s residents hardy and plain people, but rejects the idea that they were isolated villagers. They had daily contact with Jews in David-Horodok and met a variety of business people through their work. The settlement brought in good teachers for its children, who, the account says, were willing to go there. These details reveal an ongoing exchange: Nirtshe had its own household economy and community life, while David-Horodok offered a nearby centre of social, educational and commercial connection.

The broader setting was [Polesia](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_0d65083dae9817bf786f36df), a region of waterways, forests and settlements linked by overland and river routes. The book’s account of Nirtshe shows how a small community could occupy a distinct place within that world: close enough to David-Horodok for regular contact, yet positioned at the river mouth to serve traffic moving through the region. The memorial book does not describe Nirtshe’s institutions in the same detail as the town’s, so it would be misleading to assume that it possessed the same communal structures. What it does record is a community with teachers, family livelihoods and sustained ties to its larger neighbour.

## The Radziwill estate and the end of Nirtshe

The residents did not own the land on which they lived and worked. The memorial book says it belonged to [Prince Radziwill](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_00c6639f5c09a79ffe3475bf), and that the Jews paid rent. In 1906, according to the book, the prince selected Nirtshe as the site of a sawmill. The residents tried to overturn the decision but failed. They received compensation and left for David-Horodok.

The book describes the move as a painful uprooting. Families had to find new livelihoods and begin again in town, though they used the compensation to buy houses and later became involved in David-Horodok’s life. In retrospect, the account notes, they may have escaped a later flight without compensation: when war came in 1914, Nirtshe’s former residents would have had to flee anyway. The sawmill, meanwhile, did not prosper and eventually closed. That judgment belongs to the memorial book’s retrospective account; the independent sources consulted do not establish the mill’s operating history.

A community that the book says had grown to about one hundred people was thus absorbed into the nearby town. The book describes the group as descendants of Yosel Morbatshik, but its spellings vary: elsewhere the founder’s name appears as Joseph Maravtchik or Yosel Maravtchik, and the family as Morbatshik or Murawtshik. These may reflect different transliterations of the same names, but they should not be silently treated as identical spellings in every record. The book supplies no detailed family tree, and its collective account cannot tell us whether every relative or descendant moved to David-Horodok at the same time. The [family’s migration to David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_96abf995471a9288328e21ae) is part of the community’s remembered history; [the sawmill’s site and records](research:Radziwill sawmill at Nirtshe, built around 1906) remain a promising subject for further research.

Nirtshe’s story is not merely that of a settlement that disappeared. It is a story of a community built around a river junction, whose members joined agriculture to commerce and whose work drew on the traffic of the waterways. Its residents’ eventual move to David-Horodok ended Nirtshe as a separate Jewish settlement, but carried its people—and their ties, skills and memories—into the town.
